title: Race and Ethnicity
in30Seconds: Race and ethnicity are social categories, not biological ones. Race refers to the physical traits a society treats as significant; ethnicity refers to shared culture and heritage. The two are often confused, but they are distinct. Sociologists also separate prejudice, an attitude, from discrimination, an action, and describe racism as prejudice and discrimination backed by the power of a dominant group, sometimes built into whole systems. Minority groups are defined by less power, not fewer numbers. The categories are invented; their effects are real.
whyItMatters: These words are used loosely long before they appear in a classroom, and loose use hides how the social world works. A manager's private belief and her hiring decision are different things, and conflating them makes both harder to see. The precise terms also explain how categories that science does not support still shape real life, from census forms to housing patterns to school budgets. Because race and ethnicity sit beneath so many other social patterns, this vocabulary unlocks later lessons on stratification, poverty, gender, and more. Getting the words right is the first honest step.
learningObjectives: Define race and ethnicity using the attributed sociological definitions and explain the difference between the two concepts.
State the honest finding that race is a social construct, not a biological one, citing the rejection of biological race by mainstream social science.
Distinguish prejudice from discrimination as attitude versus action, with original examples of each.
Explain racism as prejudice and discrimination backed by the power of a dominant group, including how it operates through systems as well as between individuals.
Define minority group by lack of power rather than numbers, with an original example.
Identify assimilation, segregation, and pluralism as patterns of intergroup relations, each with one factual line and an original example.

collegeVersion.heading: Two words, two meanings: race and ethnicity
collegeVersion.body: Sociologists use race and ethnicity as distinct terms even though everyday conversation often blends them. Race, in the working definition of OpenStax's Introduction to Sociology 3e, refers to superficial physical differences that a particular society considers significant; a human race is a grouping of humankind based on shared physical or social qualities that can vary from one society to another. Historically, thinkers tried to sort humans into a fixed set of biological races; the German naturalist Johann Friedrich Blumenbach proposed five categories in the eighteenth century. Those schemes fell into disuse, and the social construction of race is now the accepted way of understanding racial categories. Ethnicity is a different idea: it is based on shared culture, the practices, norms, values, and beliefs of a group, including shared language, religion, and traditions. The two concepts cut across each other. OpenStax notes that ethnic groups such as Irish, Italian American, Russian, Jewish, and Serbian are all predominantly included in the White racial category. Original example: in the fictional town of Harborview, Maya and Elena both mark the same race box on a form, but Maya's family celebrates the Italian American Feast of the Seven Fishes on Christmas Eve while Elena's family observes the Serbian custom of Slava. Same racial category, two ethnicities.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest note: invented, but real
collegeVersion.body: Mainstream sociology is blunt on this point: race is a social construct, not a biological one. OpenStax reports that social science organizations including the American Sociological Association, the American Anthropological Association, and the American Psychological Association have all officially rejected explanations of race as biologically identifiable; earlier racial categories rested on pseudoscience and were often used to justify racist practices. The U.S. Census Bureau makes the same point in official terms: the racial categories in the census questionnaire reflect a social definition of race recognized in this country, not an attempt to define race biologically, anthropologically, or genetically, and individuals answer by self-identification. Why do invented categories matter? Because people and institutions act on them. The Census Bureau states that race data are required for many federal programs and are critical for civil rights enforcement, redistricting, equal employment opportunity, and assessing disparities in health and environmental risks. The honest framing is one sentence: race is a social invention with real effects — made by people, with measurable consequences.

collegeVersion.heading: Prejudice, discrimination, racism: attitudes, actions, systems
collegeVersion.body: The three words are often used as synonyms, and sociologists insist they are not. Prejudice refers to the beliefs, thoughts, feelings, and attitudes someone holds about a group; a prejudice is not based on personal experience, it is a prejudgment originating outside actual experience. Discrimination, by contrast, consists of actions against a group of people, based on race, ethnicity, age, religion, health, or other categories. The attitude-action split produces four combinations, which OpenStax labels unprejudiced nondiscriminators, unprejudiced discriminators, prejudiced nondiscriminators, and prejudiced discriminators. Original example: a fictional Harborview landlord privately believes that members of a certain ethnic group make unreliable tenants; that is a prejudice. If he refuses to show apartments to members of that group, he has discriminated. A manager who believes in fairness but follows an old scheduling habit that leaves one group out discriminates without holding a prejudice. Racism builds on both: OpenStax defines it as a stronger type of prejudice and discrimination used to justify inequalities by maintaining that one racial category is somehow superior or inferior to others, a set of practices used by a racial dominant group to maximize advantages for itself by disadvantaging racial minority groups. Racism also operates systemically: systemic racism, also called structural or institutional racism, is procedures and structures that disadvantage racial minority groups, such as a school system that routes students of color into underfunded schools.

collegeVersion.heading: Minority groups and the patterns between groups
collegeVersion.body: A minority group, in sociology, is not defined by numbers. Sociologist Louis Wirth (1945) defined a minority group as any group of people who, because of their physical or cultural characteristics, are singled out from the others in the society in which they live for differential and unequal treatment, and who therefore regard themselves as objects of collective discrimination. OpenStax adds the key line: being a numerical minority is not a characteristic of being a minority group; sometimes larger groups are considered minority groups because of their lack of power. Original example: in the fictional country of Valea, speakers of the southern dialect outnumber northern speakers three to one, yet courts and official schools use only the northern dialect, so southern speakers must learn it to get ahead — the larger group holds less power. Sociologists also name the patterns that form between groups. Assimilation is the process by which a minority individual or group gives up its own identity by taking on the characteristics of the dominant culture; original example: the fictional Taviran immigrant family whose grandchildren speak only English and keep just a few holiday customs. Segregation is the physical separation of two groups, particularly in residence, but also in workplace and social functions; it can be de jure, written into law, or de facto, produced by other factors. Original example: two fictional Harborview neighborhoods divided by an old rail line, with most residents of each rarely crossing it. Pluralism is the most tolerant pattern, the salad bowl ideal in which each culture retains its own identity and yet adds to the flavor of the whole, held together by mutual respect; original example: Harborview's annual market, where the city's communities each keep their own food and music while sharing one festival.

vocabulary.definition: A socially defined category based on physical traits, such as skin color or facial features, that a particular society considers significant.
Shared culture: the practices, norms, values, and beliefs of a group, including shared language, religion, and traditions.
A category invented by people and given meaning through shared social agreement, rather than one found naturally in the world.
A biased belief, thought, feeling, or attitude about a group, formed outside of direct personal experience.
Actions taken against a group of people, based on categories such as race, ethnicity, age, religion, or health.
A stronger type of prejudice and discrimination used to justify the belief that one racial category is superior or inferior to others.
A group singled out for differential and unequal treatment, defined by lack of power rather than by smaller numbers.
The process by which a minority individual or group gives up its own identity by taking on the characteristics of the dominant culture.
The physical separation of two groups, particularly in residence, but also in workplace and social functions.
A pattern of intergroup relations in which each culture retains its own identity while adding to the whole, held together by mutual respect.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Think of race and ethnicity as labels people invented to sort each other, not labels found in nature. Race sorts people by physical appearance, the way a society decides to read it; ethnicity sorts people by culture, the way they actually live: language, food, holidays, faith. Because the labels are invented, they differ from place to place and era to era; a category treated as a race in one society may not even exist in another. But an invented label can still steer real life: it can decide which apartment a landlord shows, which school a child attends, which box a form asks you to tick. Sociologists keep three pairs straight: prejudice is what someone believes, discrimination is what someone does, racism is prejudice and discrimination backed by the power of a dominant group and built into systems. And a minority group is about who holds power, not who has the numbers.
eli10.analogy: Race and ethnicity are like the lines painted on a sports field. Nobody found those white lines in nature; people drew them, and everyone agreed to play by them. The lines decide where the game happens, what counts as in bounds, and which team gets which side. Move the same game to a field drawn differently, and the lines change.
eli10.analogyLimits: The field-line analogy breaks down because lines on a field matter only during the game, and players can step off the field. Racial and ethnic categories follow people through every part of life, from forms to housing to medicine, and nobody gets to opt out of being sorted. A field's lines are also repainted fresh each season, while social categories carry centuries of history and habit that move slowly.

workedExample: The fictional Tran family left the island nation of Tavira for the city of Harborview three generations ago. Grandfather Ivo arrived speaking Taviran and wearing the green-and-gold shawl of his home region; his son learned English, took a job at the port, and married outside the community; his granddaughter Leila, born in Harborview, knows a few words of Taviran and celebrates the city's holidays instead of Taviran ones. Sociologists call that arc assimilation: each generation gave up more of the group's own identity and took on the dominant culture's. The family also shows the race-and-ethnicity distinction: Leila's race category never changed across the generations, while her ethnicity largely did.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Race and ethnicity are the same thing."
commonMistakes.correction: They are different concepts. Race is about physical traits a society considers significant; ethnicity is about shared culture and heritage. People of the same race can belong to many different ethnicities.

commonMistakes.mistake: "A minority group is a group with fewer people."
commonMistakes.correction: In sociology the defining feature is less power, not fewer numbers. A numerical majority can be a minority group if it lacks power in society.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Prejudice and discrimination are two words for the same behavior."
commonMistakes.correction: Prejudice is an attitude, a prejudgment formed outside experience; discrimination is an action. People can hold a prejudice and never act on it, and people can discriminate without holding a prejudice.

commonMistakes.mistake: "If race is a social construct, it is not real, so it does not matter."
commonMistakes.correction: Socially constructed categories have very real consequences. The categories were invented by people, but institutions act on them every day, and the effects are measurable.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Racism is only individual acts, like slurs."
commonMistakes.correction: Sociologists also study systemic racism: procedures and structures that disadvantage racial minority groups, which can operate even when no single individual intends them.

compareContrast.distinction: Race is a socially defined category based on physical traits a society considers significant; ethnicity is shared culture and heritage. A person's race category can stay constant across generations while ethnicity shifts.

Prejudice is an attitude, a prejudgment formed outside actual experience; discrimination is an action against a group. They can occur separately: prejudice without discrimination, and discrimination without prejudice.

Assimilation means a minority group gives up its own identity and takes on the dominant culture; pluralism means each culture keeps its identity while adding to the whole. One erases difference; the other preserves it.

keyTakeaway: Race and ethnicity are socially defined categories with real consequences; prejudice is an attitude, discrimination is an action, racism is prejudice and discrimination backed by power in systems, and a minority group is defined by less power, not fewer numbers.

questionBank.prompt: In sociology, race is best described as which of the following?
options: A socially defined category based on physical traits that a particular society considers significant.
A fixed biological classification of humans that is found in nature.
The shared culture, language, and traditions of a group of people.
A group's combined level of income, education, and occupation.
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax defines race as superficial physical differences that a particular society considers significant. Option B is the biological view that mainstream social science rejected; C describes ethnicity; D describes socioeconomic status, which belongs to a sibling topic.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the attributed sociological definition of race and rejecting the biological misconception.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement matches the sociological definition of a minority group?
options: Any group that makes up less than half of a country's population.
Any group that has recently immigrated to a country.
A group singled out for unequal treatment, defined by lack of power rather than by numbers.
A group whose members share the same native language.
questionBank.explanation: Following Wirth (1945), OpenStax defines a minority group by differential and unequal treatment, and notes that being a numerical minority is not required; lack of power is the defining characteristic. Options A, B, and D confuse size, recency, or language with power.
questionBank.skill: Recalling that minority status rests on power, not numbers.

questionBank.prompt: A rental agent in the fictional town of Harborview privately believes members of a certain ethnic group are unreliable tenants, yet he shows apartments to everyone equally and never acts on the belief. Which pair of terms describes his situation?
options: Prejudice and discrimination.
Prejudice without discrimination.
Discrimination without prejudice.
Systemic racism.
questionBank.explanation: The agent holds a biased attitude, a prejudice, but takes no actions against the group, so there is no discrimination. Discrimination requires action; systemic racism describes procedures and structures, not this individual case.
questionBank.skill: Applying the attitude-versus-action distinction to an original scenario.

questionBank.prompt: Leila was born in Harborview to a family from the fictional island of Tavira. She speaks only English, celebrates Harborview's holidays, and knows little of Taviran customs, while her grandfather still follows them all. Which pattern of intergroup relations does her story show?
options: Pluralism.
Segregation.
Racism.
Assimilation.
questionBank.explanation: Assimilation is the process by which a minority individual or group gives up its own identity by taking on the characteristics of the dominant culture, which is exactly Leila's trajectory. Pluralism would preserve Taviran identity, segregation is physical separation, and racism is prejudice and discrimination backed by power.
questionBank.skill: Applying the definition of assimilation to an original multigenerational scenario.

questionBank.prompt: A sociologist observes a region in which one group controls most positions of power even though another group is far larger in number. Why would the sociologist call the larger group a minority group?
options: Because minority always refers to a group's size.
Because the larger group has a weaker shared culture.
Because minority status is defined by lack of power, not by numbers.
Because minority groups are always immigrant groups.
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax states that being a numerical minority is not a characteristic of being a minority group; it is the lack of power that defines the subordinate position, so a larger group can be a minority group. The other options confuse size, culture, or immigration status with power.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a power-and-numbers scenario using the sociological definition of minority group.

provenance.rightsStatus: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e sections are CC BY 4.0 (facts synthesized in original wording, no text reproduced; all examples original); Census Bureau page is public-domain government content used reference-only; no source prose reproduced.
provenance.transformation: Definitions of race (superficial physical differences a society considers significant), ethnicity (shared culture), and the social construction of race with the ASA rejection of biological race verified against OpenStax Intro to Sociology 3e section 11.1 (read 2026-08-22, direct fetch of the canonical URL). Minority group per Wirth (1945) and the lack-of-power-not-numbers note verified against 11.1. Prejudice as attitude, discrimination as action, the four attitude/action combinations, racism as a stronger type of prejudice and discrimination used by a dominant racial group, and systemic racism verified against 11.3. Assimilation, segregation (de jure and de facto), and pluralism ('salad bowl') verified against 11.4. The Census Bureau's statement that census racial categories reflect a social definition, not a biological one, self-identification, and the uses of race data (civil rights, redistricting, equal employment, health and environmental disparities) verified against census.gov 'About the Topic of Race' (read 2026-08-22, direct fetch). Out-of-scope guard: fine-grained stratification and class analysis belong to sibling topics (social-stratification, social-class, poverty); cross-cultural depth on ethnicity belongs to the anthropology subject. All examples are original to this lesson.
